extracted.intended_audience: mathematicians (graduate students, postdocs, faculty) seeking career/research advice
extracted.subtask_description: Advice for mathematicians on why and how to attend seminars, talks, and conferences (including ones not directly related to their work) to advance research, networking, and motivation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Attend talks and conferences even if not directly related
rubrics_metrics.description: Title recommendation: attend talks and conferences even those not directly related to your work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Implicit guidance throughout: exposure to nearby fields and topics outside your immediate area is worthwhile; the act of attending itself yields multiple career and research benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broaden perspective
rubrics_metrics.description: Exposure to nearby fields provides valuable context for your own research.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend talks in neighboring areas to gain context and possibly new viewpoints that inform your work. Broadening perspective is listed as a core benefit of conference attendance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Build community
rubrics_metrics.description: Conferences help identify key researchers and establish collegial relationships.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use conferences to meet and recognize who works on related problems, to establish collegial relationships, and to situate yourself within the research community.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustain motivation
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attend talks to regain or maintain enthusiasm for research; hearing exciting work can sustain long-term productivity and interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Have realistic expectations for comprehension
rubrics_metrics.description: Don't expect complete comprehension of every talk: "As long as you learn something, the effort is not wasted."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that you will not fully understand every talk; measure success by whether you learn something useful rather than by full comprehension.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid isolation
rubrics_metrics.description: The overarching principle: isolation undermines breakthrough work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Actively avoid working in isolation by engaging with others at talks and conferences; collaboration and awareness of the broader field are essential to making breakthroughs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Work diligently within your field
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustained, focused effort in your core area remains a central ingredient of productive mathematics; attending events complements this diligence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Develop broad knowledge across related areas
rubrics_metrics.description: Developing broad knowledge across related areas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cultivate knowledge beyond narrow specialization by attending diverse talks; broad knowledge helps place your work in context and can spark new directions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ask questions actively and seek dialogue
rubrics_metrics.description: Asking questions actively and seeking dialogue with peers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Engage during and after talks: ask questions, start conversations, and pursue follow-up discussions to deepen understanding and build collaborations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider the larger mathematical landscape
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep an eye on how your research fits into broader themes and developments in mathematics; conferences provide perspective on the larger landscape.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine intelligence with patience and persistence
rubrics_metrics.description: Combining intelligence with patience and persistence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Long-term success requires not only ability but also persistence and patience; attending events is part of a sustained career strategy rather than a quick fix.
